articles.title: Show HN: ReVault – new secure archive format
articles.summary:
reVault is a new, secure-by-default archive format called a lockbox, designed to be simple to use.
I've been working on reVault for about 2 years. It was originally written in Dart, but with the improvements in AI, I decided to port it to Rust using AI.
It's now in beta, so I'm looking for feedback, particularly around the different language bindings.
A lockbox is encrypted, signed and compressed by default. Each can be disabled selectively.
  - Hybrid post-quantum or passphrase encryption, including metadata.
  - Zstd compression.
  - Pure Rust libraries wherever possible.

The manual is a work in progress:
https://docs.revault.onepub.dev/
reVault supports Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and arm64, plus Wasm. The core is Rust, with bindings for C/C++, Java, Dart, Python, Ruby, JS/TypeScript, Go, C#, Kotlin, Lua, PHP and Swift.
Within a lockbox you can store:
  - Files, directories, permissions and symlinks.
  - Variables.
  - Forms.

reVault uses a portable vault (just another lockbox with structured content) to hold your keys, contacts' keys, lockbox aliases and form definitions.
It ties into your platform's secure store, so logging into your desktop unlocks your vault. You don't have to enter a passphrase every time you access a lockbox. You can disable this.
There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose:
  lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox
  lbx mybox open --duration 1h
  lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE

  lbx session default mybox
  lbx var get KEY

  lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project
  lbx store.lbox mirrors update

Recovery
Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted.
Sharing
An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it.
reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental.
OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits.
To publish your default profile's public key:
  lbx vault profiles email you@example.com
  lbx vault profiles publish

  lbx vault contacts receive 
 

  lbx vault profiles fingerprint

  lbx access grant alice

To install the CLI and get started:
  cargo install revault_cli
  lbx vault init
  lbx completion install

  lbx doctor

I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

articles.title: iPhone Portrait Mode, 10 Years In
articles.summary:
Speaking of Johnnie Manzari, he wrote a post yesterday marking the 10 year anniversary of Portrait Mode:
Initially, Portrait mode was seen as a giant math problem. You’d
do disparity calculations on the two sensors and output a depth
map. The problem was this approach feels and looks digital; it
feels fake. In areas without texture, it’s impossible to do this
calculation. In areas with ultra fine detail, a lower resolution
depth map leads to terrible transitions and a full resolution
depth map takes forever to compute. One solution would be to
reduce the amount of bokeh so the issues are not as obvious. But
then you lose the whole point of the feature, which was to make it
look like you had a large, wide-open lens.
The solution to this conundrum — the tradeoff between artifacts
and the amount of blur — was quite elegant, but it took a while
to stumble across. There’s a saying in painting that if you get
the eyes right, nothing else matters. Inspired by this principle
from oil painting, the idea was to make sure we never got the
eyes wrong.
Matthew Panzarino:
I remember getting the call to test out portrait mode before its
release. The marriage of history, art and computational science
that came together to make this possible is still incredible to me
to this day.
 ★

articles.title: MacOS Extensions pack for the Apple Network Server v1.0
articles.summary:
Apple Network Server, Apple's Unix-through-and-through $10,000+ server that only shipped with, and only officially ran, Harpoon, its unique superset of IBM AIX. An ANS 500, the lower tier of this dorm fridge-sized computer, was the first server I ever personally owned, a nearly-new hand-me-down after Steve Jobs convinced Gil Amelio to cancel the machine and the bookstore's vendor at the University I worked for wouldn't support it anymore. There are several fascinating features present in Harpoon that were never implemented in any other Apple product. Currently I have three, that original ANS 500, this ANS 700 here which I use for testing, and a battery-bombed EVT prototype (a so-called "Shiner ESB" that used to be at Netscape).

The ANS was strongly based on the Power Macintosh 9500 and Apple was known to have demonstrated the ANS with Mac OS during development, but this confused potential buyers, causing the ability to boot Mac OS to be stripped from production systems. While then-CTO Ellen Hancock claimed in 1997 a ROM swap would enable the ANS to boot Mac OS again and Windows NT, these ROMs were believed to be vapourware until a former Apple employee presented a working dump of both the preproduction ROM and the later ANS Mac OS ROM. A prototype Windows NT ROM also emerged from another former employee, though there are pieces missing and booting Windows NT natively on the ANS is still a work in progress (hopefully to be the subject of a future article).

It turned out I had one of the preproduction ROMs myself and didn't realize what it was. Because the later Mac OS ROM was apparently unfinished, it doesn't properly support the L2 cache and consequently runs substantially slower, and it can't boot AIX. The preproduction ROM does boot both operating systems and does support the cache. On the other hand, it doesn't support the on-board video or the front Fast Wide SCSI-2 controller, the on-board MACE Ethernet doesn't work, and after MacOS first boots, the next restart without zapping the PRAM will come up with a black screen.

The good news is, many of the issues with the preproduction ROM in Mac OS can be fixed or worked around in software. So I've fixed or worked around many of them in software: the MACE Ethernet is fixed, the on-board video is now supported, and the ANS can restart properly back into Mac OS. Plus, because it's the preproduction ROM, you can still boot AIX, thus preserving the entire historical reason for Shiner's existence. Here's the first cut of that software and how it was developed.



Joe's Computer Museum has a few in stock (not affiliated, just a satisfied occasional customer). I tested the original design of these ROM DIMMs, kindly provided by Jeff Walther. Jeff assembled and donated this particular batch to Joe Strosnider, who is selling them and donating the proceeds in turn to the maintenance of the Tinker Different forum, where this whole thing started.

Now that you have the basic hardware, you'll then need to install Mac OS to an external bootable SCSI volume. For this project I use a 25-pin BlueSCSI which connects directly to the ANS' rear SCSI port and runs on termination power. Set up a blank disk image of the desired size to the device's (micro)SD card and rename it to the desired SCSI ID, which for the ANS is typically SCSI ID 2.

If you have another Mac with a SCSI port handy, it's easiest to do the MacOS installation to the external volume with that system. Make sure it installs Mac OS for any supported Mac, especially if you are using a model-specific installer CD; up to Mac OS 9.1 inclusive will boot directly on the ANS, and 9.1 is what I'm using here. 7.6 will work and late versions of System 7.5 might work, but I recommend at least 8.1 or later. If you only have the ANS and/or have no other suitable vintage Mac that can perform the installation, you can do it on the ANS itself with a bit more difficulty. For that you'll need to not only create the blank disk image but additionally include an ISO of a bootable MacOS CD (use ID 0), plus install a Power Mac-compatible PCI video card — I use a Twin Turbo 128MA but any ATI Mac-specific card of the era should also work, such as the Rage Orion.

Finally, unplug the server, unlock and pull open the mainboard drawer, remove the PRAM battery, install the preproduction ROM DIMM, and leave the drawer open and the system completely depowered for at least several minutes while you enjoy the droll prose of this blog post.
  


INITs and CDEVs, which is to say, the extensions and control panels which extend the operating system (and in many cases constitute substantial parts of it). Adding device support to the operating system required a DRVR resource, which could be stored in the declaration ROM of a NuBus card and available at power-on, or in an INIT or CDEV and made available during the boot process, or in a regular application and loaded on demand. (Parenthetically, desk accessories were also implemented as DRVRs.) Even after the 1994 transition to PowerPC, some, if not all, of such code still had to be 68K for backwards compatibility, and thus required emulation on a Power Macintosh.

Since this requirement was an obvious performance bottleneck, Apple attempted to address it in Copland, Apple's fallback attempt to modernise the Mac OS stepwise amid the slow-motion death marches of Taligent and PowerOpen-A/UX 4. Copland's tale of woe is a much longer story, to be the topic of a future article, but the part relevant to this piece was the new driver architecture it introduced. This aspect was part of how Copland's design partitioned its components ih memory to avoid the attendant pitfalls inherent in the classic Mac OS. In order to wall the old Mac OS world off but retain compatibility, everything that was 68K code lived in the so-called "cooperative" address space and was treated as data to be interpreted by the Power Mac 68K emulator, including 68K portions of the Toolbox. Even PowerPC-native System 7 applications ran here, since significant portions of the Toolbox were still 68K. This cooperative address space would theoretically allow most applications to run as they did before, but intentionally without privileges to the rest of the system nor access to Copland's hardware abstraction layer (HAL).
  
As such, Copland drivers necessarily were fully native code, in this case implemented as regular PowerPC code fragments. These drivers hooked into the HAL and the Name Registry, an object database that tracked devices on the system and mediated loading and unloading device drivers as needed, and were collapsed into a separate global region at a lower execution level where only limited operating system functionality was available. Although such limitations restricted their ability to integrate with the operating system, it also enabled those drivers to run early in the boot process and remain protected from user code. This new class of driver was called a native driver.

When the MacOS File Manager and Resource Manager are up, the Extensions folder is scanned for native drivers (stored as code fragments with a Type of ndrv, but otherwise the same general structure as their Copland antecessors) and handed to the expert of each particular service category for device classes the family expert supervises. Eligible and matching ndrvs, be they in ROM or on disk, are loaded before any other extension is ever invoked, and the family expert activates and wires them into the operating system.

The most important thing to notice here is that even though the Name Registry was first added to PCI Power Macs, there are many more nodes here than merely PCI cards, as there would have been in Copland. Both our PCI cards indeed do appear, connected to one of the Bandit PCI controllers (the ANS has two but mapped differently than the 9500, and there is reserved address space for up to four). Immediately before the driver name length byte is an $06. The two bits set in this byte indicate that the driver is opened as soon as it is loaded (kDriverIsOpenedUponLoad, $02), and that the family expert is responsible for doing so (kDriverIsUnderExpertControl, $04). The PCI DDK documentation states that all video drivers should set these two bits, and only these two. The family expert handling graphics drivers is hinted by the FourCCs in the next line, ndrv for a general native driver service category, and vido for the type, in this case a graphics card.

On Open Firmware 1.0.5 systems like most beige PCI Power Macs, this does nothing more than keep Open Firmware itself on the serial port; the video and ADB keyboard remain the console. On the ANS' 1.1.x firmware, however, it actually obeys these settings so that you can install and run Harpoon AIX over a serial port, and this was also apparently how Shiner NetWare ran. In this configuration the machine comes up with no video at all, though interestingly ADB devices are still useable in Mac OS, including the keyboard.

The latter two define mappings between the Open Firmware platform identifier and the respective NVRAM settings in OFpt, which is stored as a single long null-terminated string with embedded Mac $0d carriage returns. (The unreleased PowerExpress turns up in this table as the Power Macintosh 9700.) When loaded, the CDEV overwrites the NVRAM settings with the one selected by platform.

Theoretically it should be possible to binary-patch in another mapping and then add a specific script for the ANS, which with this ROM would have a platform string of AAPL,ShinerESB. ttya, it resets them back to the default kbd (ADB keyboard) and screen (onboard 54M30 video), and installs an nvramrc of its own. The critical code looks like this, using a library function I transplated to do the NVRAM patching in place:




The numbers are fixed indexes into NVRAM since this is just a hack, but in order are input-device, output-device, use-nvramrc? and nvramrc itself. This simple nvramrc patches up the Ethernet to work correctly with the Mac OS Apple Enet INIT. Prior Macintoshes with Ethernet, including first generation NuBus Power Macs like the Workgroup Server 9150, had a single Ethernet AAUI port, but AAUI was expensive and unpopular and as the industry moved to twisted-pair Apple offered both an 8P8C ("RJ-45") and AAUI port starting with the 9500 — but still using just the single MACE, so only one port was active at a time. For as yet unexplained reasons, the ANS went back to a single AAUI port with no 8P8C/"RJ-45" despite being an evolution of the same platform base.

This means the MACE is connected directly to the (A)AUI port in the ANS, whereas in machines like the 7300, 7500, 8600, 9500, etc., it switches between the AAUI (equivalent to AUI) or an internal MAU to provide the link over twisted-pair. The MACE embedded in CURIO has a register called PLSCC, or the Physical Layer Signaling Configuration Control, which determines which network port is active. In dual-ported machines, the PLSCC value should be 7 (which includes the $01 enable bit), which corresponds to the "General Purpose Serial Interface" to the circuitry where the signal is routed. In the ANS, however, this value should 1, which specifies a direct AUI connection.

The ANS Mac OS ROM internally and explicitly specifies a property PLSCCPort on /bandit/gc/mace with that value of 1. @joevt gets credit here (a) for  discovering that the Apple Enet INIT looks for and if specified uses this property as an override, relying on a platform default if not, and (b) for the magic incantation required to make this property stick when placed in the nvramrc. Since the ANS looks like a Power Mac 9500 to Mac OS, this value must be provided before Apple Enet runs, so since it's not in the 1.1.20.1 ROM we'll provide it ourselves in Open Firmware before the operating system even starts.

This scheme works and solves both the reboot-shutdown and Ethernet problems simultaneously. But what about bringing the system up from a cold start, where this property won't yet have been set? Well, we have a solution for that too!


  

The Mac OS NameRegistryLib allows us to directly manipulate the Name Registry (which will necessarily have a copy of our Open Firmware properties), so we can also get this property installed during boot as long as we do so before the Apple Enet INIT opens. We could do this with an ndrv, but we have a simpler and more conventional way which I talked about in this blog before with ways to expand virtual Mac device support in QEMU. kanjitalk755's tablet INIT installs a handler for USB HID devices during startup which allows QEMU absolute pointer positioning to work with its synthesized virtual USB tablet.

In this INIT, a block of 68K code (remember, the normal state of the Power Macintosh nanokernel is to run 68K code in the emulator) invoked at load time displays the icon and uses the Code Fragment Manager to pull a single non-static PowerPC function from the "PPC " resource (yes, P P C and a trailing space), set up a Universal Procedure Pointer to it as PowerPC native code, and run it. This code fragment is what installs the HID report handler.

Because this extension is so modular in design, we can just gut it and replace the PPC  resource with our own code (yes, PowerPC code can run from resources, not just from the data fork), though I also manually patched the 68K section with a couple NOP instructions to not bother displaying the icon since we don't really need to. This is the entirety of the PowerPC code:




Notice the device tree paths for the two devices we're interested in, Devices:device-tree:packages:aix-boot (or, as an Open Firmware path, /packages/aix-boot) and Devices:device-tree:bandit:gc:mace (/bandit/gc/mace). We don't need to know anything else about what these nodes are or how they're connected to query and modify them. The first step this function takes is to see if this is an AIX-capable ROM by checking for the AIX booter package as a Name Registry node, and if this package isn't present, such as a regular Power Mac or the ANS Mac OS ROM, then we exit. The second step is to see if the PLSCCPort property already exists; if it does, such as being set from our nvramrc, we exit also, or otherwise set the proper value of 1.

Since the whole scheme can only work if our extension runs first, we give it the special file type of scri instead of INIT, which is notionally a WorldScript extension but can be used to load any sort of extension, because WorldScript extensions load before all other INITs (Apple Enet is an INIT). Failing that, the name of the extension (ANS MACE Fixer) is intentionally chosen to lexically sort above Apple Enet so that it will also run first. The upshot is that the property will be set one way or another before the Ethernet INIT runs, and with this extension installed, now the only circumstance where our Ethernet won't work would be on the very first boot after a PRAM zap with extensions off — which would obviously be an uncommon situation.

It is also important to ensure that main() is the only non-static function in the code fragment because of the way the 68K code finds, declares and calls it (see the prior article for why). CodeWarrior's project settings can be set to build this file as a resource and after doing so we manually merge everything together in ResEdit for the final extension.

As our last stop before the installation instructions, let me also talk a little bit about something not in this version of the extensions pack.


ndrv in the ANS Mac OS ROM. Indeed, it must, or else the internal SCSI wouldn't be bootable with that ROM (the production and pre-production ROMs have their own support and hand everything over to AIX after boot). It is possible to extract this ndrv and wrap it as an extension in the same way. It won't be bootable, of course, but in theory this should allow devices on the internal SCSI to be used once Mac OS has booted from the external SCSI. Go ahead and try it. It doesn't work. The machine will boot, but no devices are visible from the internal SCSI drive bays.


Load Driver Test) where you can test the structure of an ndrv to see if it's valid (useful for hardware builders before they spend a lot of money burning defective ROMs). This utility basically checks if the ndrv can be loaded as a code fragment, and if it can, that it has a sensible driver description block, and shows the device node it's looking for and the driver name it installs.

We can immediately see from this that the node name is wrong. In the ANS Mac OS 2.0 ROM, the 53C825 nodes in the Name Registry are named apple53C8xx, not 53c825 as they are in the pre-production ROM. Triumphantly I changed the string and length byte to make the matched name 53c825. It still didn't work.


PCIPeek) which allows you to mess around with PCI-based devices. When we ask it for the PCI configuration space for one of the 53C825s using the node name 53c825, we can pull it up and see all 64 bytes are valid. Though the compatible name doesn't fetch, this does at least prove that the issue isn't the logic board and the node name is correct.


ndrvs, the documentation states SCSI ndrvs should only have a single bit set in that byte, in this case specifying that the family expert handles loading the driver (kDriverIsUnderExpertControl, $04).

Since that didn't load nor open the driver, I tried setting various bit combinations of forcing it to load upon discovery and/or open upon load, all of which ended up hanging the ANS doing boot. Remember how I said that SHIFT doesn't stop ndrvs from loading? Each of these permutations thus ended up making the external SCSI volume unbootable until the poison ndrv was removed. I had to connect it to the WallStreet PowerBook G3 (it was handy) to get it out, though as a check I had the Wally boot from the same volume just to see what it would do — and it booted fine. The driver doesn't load on the Wally almost certainly because the device name doesn't match anything, which also implies the hang is specific to trying to bring up the device on the ANS or we'd hang on the Wally too.

This leaves us at the mercy of the family expert, so the next thing I tried was various combinations of service category and type. By default this is ndrvgenr, so I tried ndrvscsi, ndrvblok, blokgenr, blokscsi, scsigenr, scsiblok, scsiscsi, blokblok and finally an intemperate combination inappropriate for a family blog, and while none of these locked up the 700, none of them made any difference either.

After all that I'm not sure this approach would have worked for getting the internal SCSI bus working anyway, at least not without additional code. Apple's PCI documentation says, "The SCSI expert is simpler than some other experts" and while it mentions the situation of a "PCI card that wants to register a SIM with the SCSI Manager" which necessarily covers the situation of one in ROM, it says nothing about disk-based drivers. It's possible the SCSI expert just doesn't handle this situation because a non-bootable SCSI bus is certainly less useful, and while we could write up an INIT to try loading the SIM manually, I'm still pondering how this would work and I have yet to find a working disk-based driver for a 53C825-based card that I could hack as an alternative (suggestions solicited in the comments). The PCI DDK 3.0 notably includes a "driver" for this chipset, but only to let you mess around with the hardware — it's intentionally not structured as a SIM, so it wouldn't be an effective foundation.

But you can still try the other pieces, so let's pick up with the install instructions now that you have the prerequisites.


on-board VGA port, not to any PCI video card, and finally power on the system. If you are using one of Jeff's current replica ROMs, you may need to hit Control-Command-Reset after powering up to get the bong (this is an electrical issue we're sorting out). From a cold start with no bootable AIX volume, the 1.1.20.1 ROM will automatically bomb into Open Firmware, showing you the prompt here. If you don't see this screen, make sure your monitor is connected to the onboard port.

If you've already prepared your external Mac OS volume and the extensions are in their proper places, just type bye at the Open Firmware ok prompt. You will see the message




while the ROM component looks for your startup disk. Once it finds it, there will be a pause, then the screen will flash and drop into the Mac OS mid-boot. Remember, the Startup Fixer must run once every time Mac OS starts up, or your system will come up with a black screen on the next boot. You can manually fix this by entering Open Firmware with a serial connection to Port 2 (38400bps, 8-N-1) and enter setenv input-device kbd, setenv output-device screen, setenv use-nvramrc? false and reset all, or you can just reset the logic board.

If you are doing an install from an external Mac OS CD-ROM or CD image, move your display to the PCI video card and then blindly type bye. You will get the Mac 50% dithered grey, then a Happy Mac, then the CD should start. Install Mac OS as usual to your previously prepared blank disk image. After the installation completes, if you can, install the extensions (e.g., from a floppy disk or via AppleShare over LocalTalk) and startup item as described above before you shut down. Either way, shut down, power off and reset your logic board again, disable or remove the CD-ROM/image, move the display back to the onboard video port, and power back on to the Open Firmware prompt. If the extensions were installed, just type bye — you're good to go. If you couldn't, move the display to the PCI card again, blindly type bye, bring up Mac OS from your external volume, install the extensions, shut down, power off and reset your logic board one last time, then move the display back to the onboard video port. Now you can boot by just typing bye also.


Get the internal SCSI bays working, which may require us to create a modified ROM and put the ndrv there with the proper node name. However, one other possibility is by installing a MacOS-bootable SCSI PCI card. The Shiner logic board has 68-pin connectors on the logic board that directly feed into the two front SCSI busses (bus 0 controls the top four trays and bus 1 controls the bottom three and the 700's rear two). These connectors were intended for the ANS PCI RAID card, but I don't see why we couldn't just connect a regular controller there as long as we change its SCSI ID to not conflict with the 53C825, which should be possible on Adaptec cards with the PowerDomain Control CDEV. I intend to do some experimentation with that, including finding an optimum card which is Mac-bootable (or flashable to same) and supports full Fast'n'Wide SCSI-2, yet is not supported by AIX so that the regular 53C825 will "just work."
On a reboot, the ANS may go into its Long RAM Test. This is not only not fatal but is arguably intended behaviour and it will start normally afterwards, though the delay is annoying. On the other hand, even though the ANS Mac OS ROM doesn't do this, it also doesn't properly register the sticks as parity RAM even if they are. I don't know if I can fix this by tweaking Open Firmware or this requires a ROM patch, though I suspect it's the latter. In the meantime, you can manually cut it short by hitting Control-Command-Reset.

a future article. For now, you can get everything on the Github repo, including source code for CodeWarrior Pro 7. Note that this compiler cannot build the 68K portion of the ANS MACE Fixer, but I've included the source for that too, and you don't need to build the 68K segment anyway merely to modify the PowerPC portion. Each portion is under its own license and you should read the brief notes. No AI was used.

articles.title: Tim Pan’s iPhone Duo Review
articles.summary:
I hadn’t heard of Tim Pan or Mediastorm until running across his 24-minute video review of the Duo. It’s a good and fair review, but what struck me are the rather astonishing production values. Amongst other things, they stress-tested the hinge with an industrial robot by opening/closing it 10,000 times. (That’s less than one-third the folds tested by Joanna Stern’s Hingey, but still.) It’s an incredible piece of work, especially given the one-week time constraint. English is Pan’s second language, and there’s an entire alternate version of the whole review, under the Mediastorm channel, in Chinese. It’s not just a different soundtrack — it’s an entirely separate cut of the video, where all his on-camera shots are spoken in Chinese.
At about 7:30 in the (English) review, Pan mentions that they (he?) offer every employee in the company a new iPhone each year. This year’s choices, by employee count:
iPhone 18 Pro: 17
iPhone 18 Pro Max: 41
iPhone Duo: 140
The point of this in the review was to show how strong demand is for the Duo amongst Pan’s company’s Chinese employees. But what struck me is that the company has 198 employees. (Last year, he says, 150 chose the 17 Pro or Pro Max; only 1 chose the Air.)  Pan’s YouTube channel includes interviews with Christopher Nolan and Hans Zimmer. I never heard of him before but he obviously didn’t come out of nowhere. (Perhaps this is only a function of how little YouTube content I watch.)
Pan only launched his X account this week. He posted the entire review video there, too, and it’s got 187,000 likes and 6,700 comments. As a promotion to launch his X account, he’s giving away 100 iPhone 18 Pros. Even if they’re base models purchased somewhere without sales tax, that’s $120,000.
Remarkable.
 ★
articles.comment: 详细且制作精良的手机评测视频观察，洞察了背后的制作与用户选择。
articles.reason: 揭示了高质量科技内容制作的幕后故事，同时涉及用户对热门苹果设备的偏好，对Apple生态感兴趣的读者有吸引力。

articles.title: Nicole Nguyen’s Duo Review for the WSJ
articles.summary:
Nicole Nguyen (also with a 5-minute video), writing for The Wall Street Journal (gift link):
Every time I used the Duo in phone mode, one-handed, I felt its
heft. It’s wider and thicker than a Pro iPhone — and heavier,
even compared with competing foldables. My hand actually hurts
after using the Duo nonstop, straining to grip the device securely
while trying to reach the far edge of the screen.
An Apple spokesman pointed to the Duo’s titanium frame for
durability. Other folding models use a lighter aluminum. The
company also moved the dock and common controls to the right to be
more reachable (sorry, southpaws). Still, there were plenty of
instances where my thumb found its limits: turning off the flash
in the camera app, or typing the letter “A.”
There are people who can easily use two hands and won’t see this
as a problem, including train commuters, frequent fliers or
parents who wait around for kids to finish their activities. For
me, I look forward to the day the Duo is lighter and thinner — maybe folding to the size of a deck of cards, like in the movie
“Her.”
Interesting that she’d prefer a smaller Duo, not a bigger one, if Apple makes a second size. I agree that one-hand-ability is a problem with the Duo, but I also think the front screen is already too squat in terms of how much content it shows. I just think it’s the nature of foldables that they’re two-handed devices, even closed.
Her’s deck of cards foldable isn’t what I think we need to wait for. It’s Westworld’s super-thin trifolds — or even a bifold that’s more along those lines of thinness.
 ★
articles.comment: 详细评测了Duo的物理特性和使用体验，特别是其重量和人体工学设计带来的不适。
articles.reason: 为潜在买家提供了关于Duo设备实用性和舒适度的重要参考，直接指出了其便携性缺陷和潜在使用痛点。

articles.title: MKBHD’s Duo Review
articles.summary:
Marques Brownlee thinks the lack of Face ID will be the biggest gripe. I agree. And I love his central framing for the review: that the Duo is extremely polished around the edges (figuratively, but also true literally) but rough in the middle.
But he spends more time griping about third-party apps that haven’t been optimized for the Duo than most other reviews, because he oddly seems to personally rely on a lot of apps from shitty iOS developers, like Discord and Google Calendar. I get it, Google Calendar is very popular. So too is Discord — it’s #6 in the App Store today for the “social networking” category. And I get it, Brownlee splits his time across iOS and Android. But Google is a notoriously terrible iOS developer. Every time there’s a major hardware display transition on iPhones that requires developer support, most of Google’s apps are late. And whatever the reasons for Discord’s popularity, it’s sure as shit not the quality of its app.
The best apps for the Duo are the best apps for iOS generally: ones that are exclusively for iOS. (And Brownlee sings the praises of several of them, too, like Carrot Weather.)
 ★
articles.comment: 总结了MKBHD对Duo的评测，强调Face ID缺失和第三方应用适配不足是主要痛点，并批评了Google的iOS应用开发质量。
articles.reason: 从知名评测人的角度分析了Duo的用户体验问题，尤其是对核心功能的缺失和应用生态的挑战，对用户购买有参考价值。

articles.title: Reuters and the WSJ on the Duo Launch
articles.summary:
Aditya Soni, Christine Chen, and Will Russell, reporting Friday for Reuters:
CEO Ternus played greeter at a store in Austin, Texas, throwing
open the doors and high-fiving customers as they streamed in, a
video ​posted on X by CBS Austin showed. A known car enthusiast,
Ternus’s Austin visit coincides with this weekend’s Formula 1 US
Grand Prix in the city, with Apple holding exclusive US broadcast
and streaming rights to the racing series.
I was wondering why Ternus and retail chief Deirdre O’Brien were in Austin for the launch. Joz held down the fort and held court at the Fifth Avenue store.
Regarding reviews:
They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks
most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended
against it for many Apple customers.
“It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it
feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished
prototype — not a finished product that I’d want to buy and
carry,” wrote longtime Apple commentator John Gruber.
Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube ​review that
for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, “it is probably
a no. But if the $2,000 doesn’t mean much to you, and you like the
idea, after the learning ​curve and getting used to not having
facial identification, it is a really fun phone.”
In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed
that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one.
Not sure Wolter set a high bar there.
Reporting for the WSJ (gift link), Rolfe Winkler quoted yours truly as well, with (IMO, and I feel I get to have an opinion here) a better line from my review:
